name: Lakota
confidence_why: Boas & Deloria 1941, Van Valin 1977, Rood & Taylor 1996 and Mirzayan 2010 all put Lakota main stress on the second syllable by rule, and differ from the catalog only in insisting that the rule has a residue of lexical exceptions (šúŋka 'dog', thípi 'house', líla 'very', rare tuktená), so second-syllable stress is secure but not exceptionless.
catalog_quote: The accent is not firmly attached to any particular syllable, but has a definite relation to the position of the syllable. In by far the greatest number of derivative forms the accent is on the second syllable; ... A large number of stems are of the form vc, cvc or ccvc ... In finite form these stems end in a and by far the greatest number have the accent on the stem syllable.
sweep_summary: Both works with stress in the title are the same work: Mirzayan 2010 (Glottolog 158234) and its 2011 citation variant (635449), the CU Boulder dissertation Lakota Intonation and Prosody. scholar.colorado.edu could not be reached by automated download), PDF 268 pp. with text taken archived copy (Internet Archive, 1 Nov 2018), saved with extracted text output, and under The work is mainly an AM intonation study, but §3.2.1 (pp. 61-63) states the word-stress facts: second-syllable stress 'for the most part' (Boas & Deloria 1941; Chambers 1978; Shaw 1980/1985 Dakota Stress Rule), many first-syllable-stressed disyllables, most rule-derived but 'synchronically genuine exceptions' remain so stress is written orthographically; §4.2.1 p. 149 'partly predictable.. generally appears on the second syllable'; §3.2.2 acoustic study confirms a lexical-stress language. Against the catalog's fixed-strict coding this contradicts strictness while confirming the dominant second-syllable pattern (consistent with our earlier reading's reclassify-to-fixed-dominant recommendation). It does not supersede Boas & Deloria 1941 as the primary description (its placement passage is a literature summary), and the better modern primary (Ullrich 2008 New Lakota Dictionary / Ullrich & Black Bear 2016 grammar) remains unheld.colorado. Glottolog, Crossref, marginalia-search, iportal.usask.ca and the the Internet Archive's index/raw download worked. No other stress-titled works exist for lako1247 in the target list.

new_statements.quote: Boas & Deloria (1941) claim that stress placement in Lakota is rule governed. For the most part the stressed vowel is the second one in the word, and generally this is also the second syllable in the word. [...] Chambers (1978) and Shaw (1980) formalize the second syllable stress assignment with a phonological rule. As exemplified even in the earlier periods of the work on Lakota grammar, however, there are many exceptions to the simple pattern of second syllable stress. [...] Despite all the proposed rules, however, there are synchronically genuine exceptions to the assignment of stress by DSR. For this reason the orthographic transcription of Lakota generally marks the location of stress.
new_statements.citation: Mirzayan, Armik. 2010. Lakota Intonation and Prosody. PhD dissertation, University of Colorado at Boulder (Linguistics Graduate Theses & Dissertations 7), 268 pp.
new_statements.locator: §3.2.1 'Previous Descriptions of Lexical Stress and Tone in Lakota', printed pp. 61-62 (pp. 81-82); corroborated by §4.2.1 p. 149 and §1.6 fn. 9 p. 25
new_statements.reading: Lakota has lexical word stress, dominantly on the second syllable (Shaw's Dakota Stress Rule: right-strong binary foot at the left word edge; prefixation keeps stress on syllable 2), with a real class of first-syllable-stressed words (šúNka, wóte, thípi, líla, t'áǧe); many of these are rule-derived in lexical phonology but some are 'synchronically genuine exceptions', which is why stress is. This supports a dominant/predominant second-syllable coding and is incompatible with a strict (exceptionless) fixed: second syllable-syllable coding; it agrees with our earlier reading note recommending reclassify fixed-strict -> fixed-dominant. Mirzayan's own first-hand contribution is the acoustic study in §3.2.2 (p. 70: 'Lakota is a lexical stress language'), not a new placement rule.

new_statements.relation_note: Second-syllable default is the same placement as the catalog record (StressTyp2: second stress) and Mirzayan 2010's summary of Boas & Deloria / Chambers / Shaw; the fn. 6 first-syllable case and the apostrophe-marking convention are consistent with the existing statement's class of first-syllable-stressed words, so this is agreement with a hint of the dominant-not-strict reading rather than a refinement of substance. The work is about Teton Dakota (Lakhota) proper, the catalog's variety.
new_statements.rule_in_words: A syntax dissertation with no phonology chapter; stress appears only in an orthographic footnote and in passing. The orthographic convention presupposes that second-syllable stress is the default (it is left unmarked in disyllables, marked elsewhere, e.g. wicha'cheya, pu'za, ate'ya), fn. 6 notes a contracted wa-+i- prefix that takes word stress on the first syllable, and §3.1.2 observes that a verb + causative (-ya / -khiya) compound carries a single primary stress, on the second syllable of the whole complex, usually inside the first verb.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; p. 86 implies only one primary stress per verb+causative complex (the causative auxiliary 'does not receive a primary stress of its own').
new_statements.exceptions: Stress marked by an apostrophe when not on the second syllable of a disyllable (so first-syllable stress and longer words are marked case by case, e.g. wai'hakya). fn. 6: when wa- + i- contract, the initial syllable takes the word stress (citing Buechel 175-6, Boas & Deloria 52-4). Monosyllables and second-syllable disyllables left unmarked in citation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: Van Valin 1977 describes Lakhota (Teton Dakota), the same variety as the catalog record; his data draw on Buechel 1939 and Boas & Deloria 1941 plus his own fieldwork.

tone_statements.translation: Clean reading: 'Stress in Dakota is marked by a combination of amplitude and pitch, a stressed syllable being somewhat louder and higher in pitch than an unstressed syllable. We here attempt only to predict the location of primary and secondary stresses at the word level; the subsidiary stresses which together comprise the over-all, complex prosodic patterns characteristic of Dakota phrases and sentences are simply outside the scope of the present endeavor. Other suprasegmental phenomena, such as length and tone, are clearly non-distinctive in Dakota, and are not examined here.'

tone.quote: [p. 25, §2] Boas and Deloria (1941) note that stressed (‘accented’ in their term) syllable is not lexically determined, but rather occurs by rules. They claim that the stress is fixed on the second syllable. [...] [p. 36, §3.4] A careful observation of the recorded tokens (using Pitchworks) suggests that the primary cue of the stress in Lakhota is relatively high pitch. [...] [p. 41, §4] First, intonational peak in Lakhota falls on the stressed syllable with a pattern of L+H*. [...] Second, there is interaction between pitch accent H* and boundary tone L%, resulting in mid tone at the end of utterance. [...] Pitch accent appears to be the most perceptually salient event which marks stress and intonation at the same time.
tone.locator: §2 'Some Phonological Aspects of Stress' p. 25; §3.4 'Summary' p. 36; §4 (end, before §5 'Conclusion') p. 41
tone.summary: No lexical tone: high pitch is the primary acoustic cue of word stress, analysed as a post-lexical L+H* pitch accent on the stressed (usually second) syllable with downstep of later peaks and an L% boundary tone; i.e. a stress language with F0-cued stress, not a tone or lexical pitch accent system.

tone.translation: Clean reading: 'Stress in Dakota is marked by a combination of amplitude and pitch, a stressed syllable being somewhat louder and higher in pitch than an unstressed syllable. We here attempt only to predict the location of primary and secondary stresses at the word level; the subsidiary stresses which together comprise the over-all, complex prosodic patterns characteristic of Dakota phrases and sentences are simply outside the scope of the present endeavor. Other suprasegmental phenomena, such as length and tone, are clearly non-distinctive in Dakota, and are not examined here.'
tone.says: Explicitly non-tonal: stress is realised by amplitude plus raised pitch ('a stressed syllable being somewhat louder and higher in pitch'); 'other suprasegmental phenomena, such as length and tone, are clearly non-distinctive in Dakota'. Word stress: underlying monosyllabic stems stress their vowel, bi- or polysyllabic stems stress the second vowel (§2.7), with STRESS MOVEMENT / STRESS LAXING rules; p. 270 adds that a trisyllable with second-syllable primary stress has a mid-high-low pitch conto…
